claim: Membrane proteins such as ion channels and transporters are frequently homomeric.
source: Membrane proteins such as ion channels and transporters are frequently homomeric.
evidence: Supported by citations to Veenhoff et al., 2002 and Forrest, 2015 in the subsequent sentence discussing multimeric assemblies.

claim: Transport proteins form multimeric assemblies of identical subunits in their native state.
source: A frequently observed feature of transport proteins is that they form multimeric assemblies of identical subunits in their native state (Veenhoff et al., 2002; Forrest, 2015).
evidence: Directly supported by citations to Veenhoff et al., 2002 and Forrest, 2015.

claim: DEER and FRET spectroscopy are commonly used for detecting structural changes accompanying function in proteins.
source: These spectroscopic techniques, which are commonly used for detecting structural changes accompanying function, rely on site-specific labeling with appropriate spectroscopic probes, typically at introduced cysteine residues.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about these spectroscopic techniques.

claim: In homomeric proteins, site-specific labeling results in labeling of each individual subunit, which complicates spectroscopic measurements.
source: In homomeric proteins, such efforts result in the labeling of each of the individual subunits and therefore the presence of multiple probes in the protein, which can complicate the spectroscopic measurements.
evidence: Logical inference from the nature of homomeric proteins and labeling procedures.

claim: It is not feasible to label a single subunit in a homomeric protein using standard approaches.
source: It is also not feasible to label a single subunit in a homomeric protein, which hinders the use of these spectroscopic approaches for investigating the structural changes that take place within individual subunits.
evidence: Based on the inherent properties of homomeric proteins where all subunits are identical.

claim: Concatenation approach has been widely used for expression of heteromeric ion channels in Xenopus oocytes for functional studies.
source: This approach has been widely used for the expression of heteromeric ion channels in Xenopus oocytes for functional studies (Gordon and Zagotta, 1995; Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon and Zagotta, 1995 and Yang et al., 1997.

claim: There are only a few examples where multimeric membrane proteins encoded in a single polypeptide have been purified for functional and spectroscopic studies.
source: There are only a few examples where multimeric membrane proteins encoded in a single polypeptide have been purified for functional and spectroscopic studies (Raghuraman et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2016; Last et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Concatenation and co-expression approaches for cellular expression of heteromeric proteins frequently suffer from very low yields.
source: Both of these approaches frequently suffer from very low yields.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of existing approaches.

claim: Refolding of membrane proteins is very challenging.
source: However, refolding of membrane proteins is very challenging, and there are only few reports in the literature (Neumann et al., 2014; Popot, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: GltPh is a homo-trimeric sodium coupled aspartate transporter.
source: To develop a protocol for the in vitro reassembly of multimeric membrane proteins, we initially focused on GltPh, a homo-trimeric sodium coupled aspartate transporter (Figure 1A)(Yernool et al., 2004; Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations and structural representation in Figure 1A.

claim: Each subunit of GltPh has eight transmembrane and two reentrant hairpin segments.
source: Each subunit of GltPh has a complex topology with eight transmembrane and two reentrant hairpin segments.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of GltPh.

claim: GltPh has been successfully refolded from a completely unfolded state using lipid vesicles to obtain an active native-like protein.
source: Remarkably, we have previously successfully refolded GltPh from a completely unfolded state by using lipid vesicles to obtain an active native-like protein (Focke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Focke et al., 2015.

claim: GltPh migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE.
source: GltPh migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE, suggesting that SDS dissociates GltPh into subunits (Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental observation.

claim: SDS dissociates GltPh into subunits.
source: GltPh migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE, suggesting that SDS dissociates GltPh into subunits (Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: Inference from SDS-PAGE migration pattern and supported by citation.

claim: Glutaraldehyde cross-linking confirmed complete dissociation of the trimeric GltPh species by SDS.
source: Glutaraldehyde cross-linking confirmed complete dissociation of the trimeric species by SDS (Focke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Crosslinking of native GltPh gives a protein band on SDS-PAGE corresponding to the trimer.
source: While crosslinking of the native GltPh gives a protein band on SDS-PAGE corresponding to the trimer, crosslinking following SDS treatment only yields monomers.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Crosslinking following SDS treatment of GltPh only yields monomers.
source: While crosslinking of the native GltPh gives a protein band on SDS-PAGE corresponding to the trimer, crosslinking following SDS treatment only yields monomers.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Glutaraldehyde crosslinking following reassembly showed the presence of a trimeric band indicating subunit reassociation.
source: Consequent glutaraldehyde crosslinking showed the presence of a trimeric band indicating subunit reassociation.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: The SEC elution profile for r-GltPh was similar to that of native GltPh.
source: The SEC elution profile for r-GltPh was similar to that of native GltPh and crosslinking confirmed the trimeric state of r-GltPh (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Crosslinking confirmed the trimeric state of r-GltPh.
source: The SEC elution profile for r-GltPh was similar to that of native GltPh and crosslinking confirmed the trimeric state of r-GltPh (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Lipid vesicles were required for the reassociation process of GltPh.
source: Lipid vesicles were required for the reassociation process, and dilution of the SDS-dissociated GltPh subunits directly into DDM did not yield a trimeric species, as indicted by both SEC and cross-linking (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing reassembly in lipid vesicles versus DDM.

claim: Dilution of SDS-dissociated GltPh subunits directly into DDM did not yield a trimeric species.
source: Lipid vesicles were required for the reassociation process, and dilution of the SDS-dissociated GltPh subunits directly into DDM did not yield a trimeric species, as indicted by both SEC and cross-linking (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Asp dissociation constant (KD) of the reassembled L130W mutant of GltPh was 216 ± 15 nM.
source: Solid lines are fits to the data using the equation described in Materials and methods with KD values of 183 ± 16 nM for native GltPh and 216 ± 15 nM for r-GltPh.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Asp dissociation constant (KD) of native L130W GltPh was 183 ± 16 nM.
source: Solid lines are fits to the data using the equation described in Materials and methods with KD values of 183 ± 16 nM for native GltPh and 216 ± 15 nM for r-GltPh.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Asp dissociation constant of reassembled L130W mutant of GltPh was similar to that of the transporter prior to the dissociation/reassociation procedure.
source: The Asp dissociation constant (KD) of the reassembled L130W mutant of GltPh was similar to that of the transporter prior to the dissociation/reassociation procedure (Figure 1D).
evidence: Comparison of KD values from experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: r-GltPh mediated uptake of [14C]Asp into proteoliposomes in the presence of an inwardly directed Na+ gradient.
source: We reconstituted r-GltPh into lipid vesicles to measure transport activity and observed uptake of [14C]Asp into proteoliposomes in the presence of an inwardly directed Na+ gradient (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The specific transport activity observed for r-GltPh was similar to that of the native transporter.
source: The specific transport activity observed for r-GltPh was similar to that of the native transporter.
evidence: Comparison of transport data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The key conformational transition of GltPh that underlies substrate translocation is an elevator-like movement of the peripherally located transport domain within each protomer relative to the central trimerization domain.
source: The key conformational transition of GltPh that underlies substrate translocation across the membrane is an elevator-like movement of the peripherally located transport domain within each protomer relative to the central trimerization domain (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reyes et al., 2009.

claim: Single-molecule FRET was previously used to visualize elevator-like movements in GltPh in real time.
source: Previously, single-molecule FRET (smFRET) was used to visualize these movements in real time (Akyuz et al., 2013; Erkens et al., 2013; Akyuz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: smFRET experiments suggested that the transition frequency determined the overall rate of substrate transport in GltPh.
source: These experiments further suggested that the transition frequency determined the overall rate of substrate transport.
evidence: Based on previous smFRET studies cited.

claim: r-GltPh in the presence of 200 mM Na+ and 100 μM Asp sampled three FRET efficiency states: low-, intermediate- and high-FRET centered at ~0.35, ~0.55 and ~0.8, respectively.
source: We found that r-GltPh in the presence of 200 mM Na+ and 100 μM Asp, sampled three FRET efficiency states, low-, intermediate- and high-FRET centered at ~0.35, ~0.55 and ~0.8, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar FRET efficiency states were observed for the native GltPh protein.
source: Similar FRET efficiency states were observed for the native protein, where the low-FRET state was attributed largely to the outward facing state of the transporter.
evidence: Comparison with previous data on native protein.

claim: The low-FRET state in GltPh was attributed largely to the outward facing state of the transporter.
source: Similar FRET efficiency states were observed for the native protein, where the low-FRET state was attributed largely to the outward facing state of the transporter.
evidence: Based on previous structural and functional studies cited (Akyuz et al., 2013).

claim: Excursions into the higher-FRET states reflect sampling of the inward-facing conformations in GltPh.
source: Excursions into the higher-FRET states reflect sampling of the inward-facing conformations (Akyuz et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: The populations of the low-, intermediate-, and high-FRET states for r-GltPh were 76%, 17% and 7%, respectively.
source: The populations of the low-, intermediate-, and high-FRET states for the r-GltPh were 76%, 17% and 7%, respectively, in good agreement with the values observed for the native transporter (71%, 16% and 13%, respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from smFRET measurements.

claim: The populations of the low-, intermediate-, and high-FRET states for native GltPh were 71%, 16% and 13%, respectively.
source: The populations of the low-, intermediate-, and high-FRET states for the r-GltPh were 76%, 17% and 7%, respectively, in good agreement with the values observed for the native transporter (71%, 16% and 13%, respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from smFRET measurements.

claim: r-GltPh exhibits conformational transitions at a rate of ~0.03/s.
source: Transition density plots showed that the r-GltPh exhibit conformational transitions at a rate of ~0.03/s, also in good agreement with the transition frequency of the native transporter (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The transition frequency of r-GltPh is in good agreement with the transition frequency of the native transporter.
source: Transition density plots showed that the r-GltPh exhibit conformational transitions at a rate of ~0.03/s, also in good agreement with the transition frequency of the native transporter (Figure 2C).
evidence: Comparison of experimental data.

claim: The FRET-state lifetimes were similar in the native and reassembled GltPh transporters.
source: In line with these findings, the FRET-state lifetimes were similar in the native and reassembled transporters (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The reassembled GltPh transporter samples the outward- and inward-facing state with probabilities and frequency similar to the native protein.
source: These smFRET measurements suggest that the reassembled transporter samples the outward- and inward-facing state with probabilities and frequency similar to the native protein.
evidence: Inference from smFRET data comparing native and reassembled protein.

claim: r-GltPh is structurally, functionally and dynamically similar to the native transporter.
source: Collectively, these results show that r-GltPh is structurally, functionally and dynamically similar to the native transporter.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental results including SEC, crosslinking, binding assays, transport assays, and smFRET.

claim: Several lines of evidence suggest that subunits in the glutamate transporter trimer are independent of each other.
source: In glutamate transporters, several lines of evidence suggest that subunits in the trimer are independent of each other (Koch and Larsson, 2005; Grewer et al., 2005; Erkens et al., 2013; Ruan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The R397A mutation lowers Asp affinity in GltPh by approximately a thousand fold.
source: The test subunits were either wild type or carried the R397A mutation, which lowers Asp affinity by approximately a thousand fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)(Verdon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: At a 10:1 ratio of test to reporter subunits, random mixing ensures that the majority of transporters assembled will contain either no reporter subunits (73%) or only one reporter subunit (24%).
source: At this ratio, a random mixing of the subunits ensures that the majority of the transporters assembled will contain either no reporter subunits (73%) or only one reporter subunit (24%), while the fraction with two or three reporter subunits will be negligibly small (3% and, 0.1% respectively).
evidence: Based on statistical calculation of random assembly.

claim: The KD value for Asp binding to heteromeric GltPh with wild type test subunits was 455 ± 61 nM.
source: The solid lines indicate fits to the data using a Hill equation with KD = 455 ± 61 nM, Hill coefficient = 0.84 ± 0.08 for the heterotrimer with the wild-type test subunits and with KD = 356 ± 36 nM, Hill coefficient = 1.05 ± 0.07 for the heterotrimer with test subunits carrying the R397A substitution.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The KD value for Asp binding to heteromeric GltPh with R397A test subunits was 356 ± 36 nM.
source: The solid lines indicate fits to the data using a Hill equation with KD = 455 ± 61 nM, Hill coefficient = 0.84 ± 0.08 for the heterotrimer with the wild-type test subunits and with KD = 356 ± 36 nM, Hill coefficient = 1.05 ± 0.07 for the heterotrimer with test subunits carrying the R397A substitution.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Hill coefficient for Asp binding to heteromeric GltPh with wild type test subunits was 0.84 ± 0.08.
source: The solid lines indicate fits to the data using a Hill equation with KD = 455 ± 61 nM, Hill coefficient = 0.84 ± 0.08 for the heterotrimer with the wild-type test subunits and with KD = 356 ± 36 nM, Hill coefficient = 1.05 ± 0.07 for the heterotrimer with test subunits carrying the R397A substitution.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Hill coefficient for Asp binding to heteromeric GltPh with R397A test subunits was 1.05 ± 0.07.
source: The solid lines indicate fits to the data using a Hill equation with KD = 455 ± 61 nM, Hill coefficient = 0.84 ± 0.08 for the heterotrimer with the wild-type test subunits and with KD = 356 ± 36 nM, Hill coefficient = 1.05 ± 0.07 for the heterotrimer with test subunits carrying the R397A substitution.
evidence: Experimental data and fitting shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expected affinity of the R397A mutant in the presence of 10 mM Na+ ions is approximately 238 µM.
source: Notably, the expected affinity of the R397A mutant in the presence of 10 mM Na+ ions is approximately 238 µM, suggesting that the R397A mutant test subunits remain largely unbound to Asp throughout the titration.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The R397A mutant test subunits remain largely unbound to Asp throughout the titration in the heteromeric binding experiment.
source: Notably, the expected affinity of the R397A mutant in the presence of 10 mM Na+ ions is approximately 238 µM, suggesting that the R397A mutant test subunits remain largely unbound to Asp throughout the titration.
evidence: Inference from the KD value and experimental conditions.

claim: Asp binding to the test subunits does not affect Asp binding to the reporter subunit in GltPh.
source: This result indicates that Asp binding to the test subunits does not affect Asp binding to the reporter subunit.
evidence: Inference from the similar KD values obtained for heteromers with wild type and R397A test subunits.

claim: There is a lack of coupling in substrate binding to the trimeric transporter GltPh.
source: Therefore, for the first time, we directly demonstrate the lack of coupling in substrate binding to the trimeric transporter GltPh.
evidence: Conclusion from the heteromeric binding experiments.

claim: DEER spectroscopy has been widely applied to follow conformational changes in membrane transporters.
source: It has been widely applied to follow conformational changes in membrane transporters. (Borbat et al., 2007; Hänelt et al., 2013; Georgieva et al., 2013; Dastvan et al., 2016; Khantwal et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The use of DEER spectroscopy for distance measurements in transporters comprised of more than two subunits is problematic because these proteins present multi-spin systems if spin-labeled using standard approaches.
source: The use of DEER spectroscopy for distance measurements in transporters comprised of more than two subunits is problematic, however, as these proteins present multi-spin systems if spin-labeled using standard approaches (Endeward et al., 2009; Dalmas et al., 2012; Georgieva et al., 2013; Hänelt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about multi-spin systems.

claim: The key transition in GltPh involves the movement of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain by as much as 15 Å.
source: In GltPh, the key transition involves the movement of the transport domain relative to the scaffold domain by as much as 15 Å.
evidence: Based on structural studies of GltPh.

claim: Introduction of Cys mutations into the scaffold and transport domains and subsequent labeling of GltPh yields six spin labels per the trimeric protein.
source: However, the introduction of Cys mutations into each domain and subsequent labeling of GltPh yields six spin labels per the trimeric protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: Logical inference from the trimeric structure and labeling strategy, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: With all subunits in the outward-facing state, up to five unique distances between spin labels are expected in homotrimeric GltPh.
source: In the simplest case, with all subunits being in the outward-facing state, we expect up to five unique distances between spin labels, depending on symmetry.
evidence: Inference from the geometry of the trimeric structure.

claim: Distance distributions generated from DEER signals of homotrimeric GltPh are very broad and difficult to extract.
source: Consequently, the distance distributions, generated from DEER signals, are very broad and difficult to extract, being further complicated by non-linear effects (Jeschke et al., 2009) and less than ideal spin-labelling efficiency.
evidence: Based on experimental challenges and cited reference.

claim: Homomeric V216C/I294C mutant GltPh in the presence of Na+ ions and Asp yielded broad weakly structured distance distributions spanning the distance range from ca. 40 to 70 Å.
source: In the presence of Na+ ions and Asp, homomeric V216C/I294C mutant yielded, as expected, broad weakly structured distance distributions, spanning the distance range from ca. 40 to 70 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental DEER data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Heteromeric GltPh with a single labeled subunit exhibited a single narrow peak at 52 Å in DEER measurements.
source: In contrast, the heteromeric protein exhibited a single narrow peak at 52 Å.
evidence: Experimental DEER data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, the V216C/I294C mutant subunit predominantly populates the inward facing state.
source: Remarkably, these measurements suggest that under our experimental conditions the V216C/I294C mutant subunit predominantly populates the inward facing state.
evidence: Inference from DEER distance measurements compared to crystallographic models.

claim: In the inward facing state of GltPh, the Cα-Cα distance between residues 216 and 294 is 48 Å based on the crystallographic model.
source: In this conformational state, the Cα-Cα distance between residues 216 and 294 is 48 Å based on the crystallographic model, in good agreement with the DEER measurement.
evidence: Based on crystallographic structural data.

claim: The Cα-Cα distance between residues 216 and 294 in the outward facing state of GltPh is 34 Å.
source: The corresponding distance in the outward facing state is 34 Å.
evidence: Based on crystallographic structural data.

claim: Using a heteromeric trimer greatly simplified the experimentally obtained distance distributions in DEER spectroscopy.
source: In conclusion, using a heteromeric trimer greatly simplified the experimentally obtained distance distributions and allowed for straightforward determination of the conformational state of the labeled protomer.
evidence: Comparison of DEER data from homomeric and heteromeric GltPh.

claim: Using heteromeric trimers allowed for straightforward determination of the conformational state of the labeled protomer.
source: In conclusion, using a heteromeric trimer greatly simplified the experimentally obtained distance distributions and allowed for straightforward determination of the conformational state of the labeled protomer.
evidence: Demonstrated by the DEER experiments comparing homomeric and heteromeric GltPh.

claim: GltSm is a glutamate transporter homolog from Staphylothermus marinus that shares 58% sequence identity to GltPh.
source: To investigate whether our in vitro subunit reassembly procedure is applicable to other multimeric transporters, we initially tested the procedure on GltSm, a glutamate transporter homolog from Staphylothermus marinus that shares 58% sequence identity to GltPh (Figure 5A)(Jaehme and Michel, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation and sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SDS dissociated the GltSm transporter.
source: We observed that SDS dissociated the GltSm transporter and that the dissociated subunits can be reassembled back to the trimeric state upon dilution of SDS coupled with protein incorporation into lipid vesicles (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Dissociated GltSm subunits can be reassembled back to the trimeric state upon dilution of SDS coupled with protein incorporation into lipid vesicles.
source: We observed that SDS dissociated the GltSm transporter and that the dissociated subunits can be reassembled back to the trimeric state upon dilution of SDS coupled with protein incorporation into lipid vesicles (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reassembled GltSm transporter was functionally similar to the native protein.
source: The reassembled GltSm transporter was functionally similar to the native protein, suggesting that the disassembly/reassembly procedure was well tolerated by GltSm, similar to GltPh (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental transport data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VcINDY is a homo-dimeric Na+-coupled succinate transporter.
source: VcINDY is a homo-dimeric Na+- coupled succinate transporter (Figure 6A)(Mancusso et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation and structural representation in Figure 6A.

claim: Each subunit of VcINDY consists of 11 transmembrane helices that are arranged in two domains, a scaffold dimerization domain and a peripheral transport domain.
source: Each subunit of VcINDY consists of 11 transmembrane helices that are arranged in two domains, a scaffold dimerization domain and a peripheral transport domain.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of VcINDY.

claim: The transport mechanism in VcINDY involves an elevator-like movement of the transport domain with respect to the scaffold domain.
source: The transport mechanism in VcINDY involves an elevator-like movement of the transport domain with respect to the scaffold domain (Mulligan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mulligan et al., 2016.

claim: The topology and fold of the VcINDY transporter is very distinct from GltPh.
source: While the elevator mechanism of VcINDY is reminiscent of the mechanism in GltPh, the topology and fold of the VcINDY transporter is very distinct (Drew and Boudker, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation and structural comparison.

claim: VcINDY is dimeric in the native state but migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE.
source: The VcINDY transporter is dimeric in the native state but migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE, indicating that SDS dissociates the transporter into monomers (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SDS dissociates VcINDY into monomers.
source: The VcINDY transporter is dimeric in the native state but migrates as a monomer on SDS-PAGE, indicating that SDS dissociates the transporter into monomers (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inference from SDS-PAGE migration pattern shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Crosslinked native VcINDY runs as a dimer on SDS-PAGE.
source: Crosslinked native VcINDY runs as a dimer on SDS-PAGE while VcINDY crosslinked after dissociation by SDS runs as a monomer.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: VcINDY crosslinked after dissociation by SDS runs as a monomer on SDS-PAGE.
source: Crosslinked native VcINDY runs as a dimer on SDS-PAGE while VcINDY crosslinked after dissociation by SDS runs as a monomer.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Crosslinking following reassembly of VcINDY in lipid vesicles yielded a dimeric species.
source: As anticipated, crosslinking following reassembly in lipid vesicles yielded a dimeric species.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6C inset.

claim: r-VcINDY had a similar SEC elution profile to the native transporter.
source: Analysis by SEC showed that r-VcINDY had a similar elution profile to the native transporter (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: r-VcINDY reconstituted into lipid vesicles mediated succinate uptake in the presence of a Na+ ion gradient with a rate similar to the native transporter.
source: The r-VcINDY transporter reconstituted into lipid vesicles mediated succinate uptake in the presence of a Na+ ion gradient with a rate similar to the native transporter (Figure 6D).
evidence: Experimental transport data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CLC-ec1 is a Cl-/H+ antiporter.
source: CLC-ec1 is a Cl-/H+ antiporter; it is a homodimeric protein in which each subunit consists of 18 helical segments (Figure 7A)(Dutzler et al., 2002; Accardi and Miller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations and structural representation in Figure 7A.

claim: CLC-ec1 is a homodimeric protein in which each subunit consists of 18 helical segments.
source: CLC-ec1 is a Cl-/H+ antiporter; it is a homodimeric protein in which each subunit consists of 18 helical segments (Figure 7A)(Dutzler et al., 2002; Accardi and Miller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations and structural knowledge.

claim: The CLC-ec1 fold has an internal antiparallel structural repeat with the N-terminal nine helical segments structurally related to the C-terminal segments.
source: The CLC-ec1 fold has an internal antiparallel structural repeat with the N-terminal nine helical segments structurally related to the C-terminal segments.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of CLC-ec1.

claim: CLC-ec1 is one of the strongest membrane protein complexes known.
source: Studies on the dimerization of CLC-ec1 have shown that it is one of the strongest membrane protein complexes known (Chadda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chadda et al., 2016.

claim: When lyophilized CLC-ec1 protein was solubilized in 1% SDS, it migrated as a homogeneous monomer on SDS PAGE.
source: When the lyophilized protein was solubilized in 1% SDS, it migrated as a homogeneous monomer on SDS PAGE.
evidence: Experimental observation.

claim: Glutaraldehyde cross-linking following incorporation of CLC-ec1 into lipid vesicles indicated the formation of dimers.
source: Following incorporation into lipid vesicles, glutaraldehyde cross-linking indicated the formation of dimers, suggesting the successful reassembly of CLC-ec1.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 7B inset.

claim: SEC of r-CLC-ec1 produced an elution profile that was similar to the native CLC-ec1.
source: SEC of r-CLC-ec1 produced an elution profile that was similar to the native CLC-ec1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The intrinsic fluorescence spectra of native CLC-ec1 shows an emission maxima at 333 nm.
source: The intrinsic fluorescence spectra of the native CLC-ec1 shows an emission maxima at 333 nm (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Addition of SDS to native CLC-ec1 results in a 46% decrease in fluorescence intensity.
source: Addition of SDS results in a 46% decrease in fluorescence intensity.
evidence: Experimental observation from fluorescence spectra in Figure 7C.

claim: The fluorescence spectra of r-CLC-ec1 was similar to the native protein.
source: The fluorescence spectra of the r-CLC-ec1 was similar to the native protein and showed a similar decrease in fluorescence intensity on the addition of SDS.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: r-CLC-ec1 showed a similar decrease in fluorescence intensity on the addition of SDS as native CLC-ec1.
source: The fluorescence spectra of the r-CLC-ec1 was similar to the native protein and showed a similar decrease in fluorescence intensity on the addition of SDS.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: r-CLC-ec1 reconstituted into lipid vesicles mediated chloride flux activity similar to the native protein.
source: The r-CLC-ec1 transporter reconstituted into lipid-vesicles-mediated chloride flux activity similar to the native protein (Figure 7D) suggesting that a fully functional transporter has been reassembled.
evidence: Experimental transport data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A fully functional CLC-ec1 transporter has been reassembled.
source: The r-CLC-ec1 transporter reconstituted into lipid-vesicles-mediated chloride flux activity similar to the native protein (Figure 7D) suggesting that a fully functional transporter has been reassembled.
evidence: Inference from functional assay data in Figure 7D.

claim: The method for in vitro reassembly involves the assembly of multimeric proteins from dissociated subunits in the context of lipid vesicles.
source: The method involves the assembly of the multimeric proteins from dissociated subunits in the context of lipid vesicles.
evidence: Summary of the methodology described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Heteromeric proteins are obtained simply by mixing wild-type and mutant subunits.
source: Heteromeric proteins are obtained simply by mixing wild-type and mutant subunits.
evidence: Description of the methodology.

claim: The reassembled transporters are indistinguishable from native proteins using biochemical, functional and single molecule approaches.
source: Using biochemical, functional and single molecule approaches, we show that the reassembled transporters are indistinguishable from native proteins.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hill coefficients greater or less than unity suggest, respectively, positive or negative cooperativity between binding sites.
source: The Hill coefficients that are greater or less than unity suggest, respectively, positive or negative cooperativity between the binding sites.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Hill coefficients.

claim: Hill coefficients are relatively poorly determined and can be affected by baseline drifts and noise in the data.
source: However, Hill coefficients are relatively poorly determined and can be affected by baseline drifts and noise in the data.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about limitations of Hill coefficient analysis.

claim: The substrate-binding sites in GltPh are uncoupled.
source: Using this approach, we show that binding to the adjacent test subunits does not affect Asp binding to the reporter subunit thereby establishing unambiguously that the substrate-binding sites in GltPh are uncoupled.
evidence: Conclusion from the heteromeric binding experiments.

claim: Some transporters are assembled from multiple subunits with substrate-binding sites located at the interfaces, for example, the EmrE and the semi-SWEET transporters.
source: Interestingly, some transporters are assembled from multiple subunits with substrate-binding sites located at the interfaces, for example, the EmrE and the semi-SWEET transporters (Chen et al., 2007; Latorraca et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: DEER spectroscopy and smFRET microscopy have been applied to study conformational flexibility and dynamics of diverse systems.
source: DEER spectroscopy and smFRET microscopy specifically have been applied to study conformational flexibility and dynamics of diverse systems (Joo et al., 2008; McHaourab et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: Many successful DEER and FRET experiments on multimeric proteins relied on measurements of inter-subunit distance changes.
source: Thus, many of the successful experiments relied on measurements of inter-subunit distance changes (Zou et al., 2009; Georgieva et al., 2013; Hänelt et al., 2013; Dastvan et al., 2016; Khantwal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The ability to assemble a multimeric system with single reporter subunits bearing cysteine mutations would significantly expand the repertoire of useful experiments.
source: The ability to assemble a multimeric system of interest with single reporter subunits bearing cysteine mutations would significantly expand the repertoire of useful experiments and also facilitate and simplify analysis.
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated advantages of heteromeric proteins.

claim: The distance distribution obtained for heteromeric GltPh bearing a single labeled subunit is dramatically simplified compared to a homomeric labeled protein.
source: Indeed, the distance distribution that was obtained for heteromeric GltPh bearing a single labeled subunit is dramatically simplified compared to a homomeric labeled protein, and allows facile determination of the conformational state of the labeled subunit.
evidence: Demonstrated by DEER data in Figure 4B.

claim: Heteromeric transporters allow facile determination of the conformational state of the labeled subunit in DEER spectroscopy.
source: Indeed, the distance distribution that was obtained for heteromeric GltPh bearing a single labeled subunit is dramatically simplified compared to a homomeric labeled protein, and allows facile determination of the conformational state of the labeled subunit.
evidence: Demonstrated by DEER data in Figure 4B.

claim: Many ion channels are homomeric in nature.
source: Many ion channels are homomeric in nature.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about ion channel structure.

claim: Ion channels transition between different conformational states during function.
source: Ion channels transition between different conformational states during function.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about ion channel function.

claim: SDS is not a strong denaturant for most membrane proteins.
source: SDS is not a strong denaturant for most membrane proteins and therefore we expect that the SDS-dissociated subunits are only partially unfolded (Harris and Booth, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris and Booth, 2012.

claim: The SDS-dissociated subunits are only partially unfolded.
source: SDS is not a strong denaturant for most membrane proteins and therefore we expect that the SDS-dissociated subunits are only partially unfolded (Harris and Booth, 2012).
evidence: Inference based on the properties of SDS and citation.

claim: Following stringent dissociation protocol, successful reassembly was observed for only GltPh and CLC-ec1, while VcINDY and GltSm could not be reassembled.
source: Following this stringent dissociation protocol, we were able to observe successful reassembly for only two of the proteins in our test set, GltPh and CLC-ec1 while VcINDY and GltSm could not be reassembled.
evidence: Experimental observation from testing different dissociation protocols.

claim: The success of the disassembly/reassembly depends on the gentle dissociation of the multimeric proteins without extensive unfolding of the subunits.
source: This observation suggests that the success of the disassembly/reassembly depends on the gentle dissociation of the multimeric proteins without extensive unfolding of the subunits.
evidence: Inference from the differential success of mild versus stringent dissociation protocols.

claim: Lipid bilayers were required for the reassociation process, and mere dilution of the SDS in the presence of mild detergents did not result in successful reassembly.
source: Further, lipid bilayers were required for the reassociation process, and a mere dilution of the SDS in the presence of mild detergents did not result in successful reassembly.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Incorporation of dissociated subunits into lipid bilayers concentrates and orients the subunits to facilitate the assembly.
source: We speculate that incorporation of the dissociated subunits into lipid bilayers concentrates and orients the subunits to facilitate the assembly.
evidence: Speculation based on the requirement for lipid vesicles.

claim: For CLC-ec1, monomers are stable.
source: For CLC-ec1, it was shown that monomers are stable (Robertson et al., 2010), and thus, it is possible that these transporters first assume a native-like fold and then assemble into dimers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2010.

claim: It is possible that CLC-ec1 transporters first assume a native-like fold and then assemble into dimers.
source: For CLC-ec1, it was shown that monomers are stable (Robertson et al., 2010), and thus, it is possible that these transporters first assume a native-like fold and then assemble into dimers.
evidence: Speculation based on the stability of CLC-ec1 monomers.

claim: Trimeric GltPh forms a bowl-like structure in the outward facing state.
source: The trimeric GltPh forms a bowl-like structure in the outward facing state (Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation and structural knowledge.

claim: The bowl in GltPh extends approximately half way across the bilayer and is lined with polar residues and is most certainly filled with water.
source: The bowl extends approximately half way across the bilayer; it is lined with polar residues and is most certainly filled with water.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of GltPh.

claim: It seems unlikely that the conformation of dissociated GltPh monomers is entirely native-like.
source: It seems unlikely that the conformation of dissociated GltPh monomers is entirely native-like because it would lead to the exposure of the polar regions of the bowl to the hydrophobic milieu of the membrane.
evidence: Inference based on structural considerations.

claim: Reaching the native conformation is likely coupled with the trimer assembly in GltPh.
source: Thus, it seems likely that reaching the native conformation is coupled with the trimer assembly in this protein.
evidence: Speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: Membrane protein assembly processes have been shown to have specific lipid requirements.

evidence: Supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2017.

claim: The ability to assemble multimeric membrane proteins in defined lipid environments will facilitate investigation of how lipid molecules participate in the multimerization process.
source: The ability to assemble multimeric membrane proteins in defined lipid environments will facilitate an investigation of how lipid molecules participate in the multimerization process.
evidence: Speculation about future applications of the methodology.

claim: The R397A substitution causes a ~1300 fold decrease in affinity for Asp binding compared to wild-type GltPh.
source: The R397A substitution (KD = 238 μM) causes a ~ 1300 fold decrease in affinity for Asp binding compared to the wild-type GltPh (KD = 0. 183 μM).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The L130W substitution in GltPh provides a spectroscopic probe for Asp binding.
source: The reporter subunit carried the L130W substitution, which provides a spectroscopic probe for Asp binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and cited in Boudker et al., 2007.

claim: An increase in fluorescence at 334 nm is observed on Asp binding by L130W GltPh.
source: An increase in fluorescence at 334 nm is observed on Asp binding by L130W GltPh.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No corresponding fluorescence change is observed for wild-type GltPh upon Asp binding.
source: No corresponding fluorescence change is observed for the wild-type GltPh.

claim: Dipolar coupling in DEER spectroscopy depends on the inter-spin distance r, as 1/r³.
source: The dipolar coupling depends on the inter-spin distance r, as 1/r3, making the method quite an accurate tool for accessing minute distance variations.
evidence: Based on the physical principles of DEER spectroscopy.

claim: DEER spectroscopy is an accurate tool for accessing minute distance variations.
source: The dipolar coupling depends on the inter-spin distance r, as 1/r3, making the method quite an accurate tool for accessing minute distance variations.
evidence: Based on the physical principles of DEER spectroscopy.

claim: Pulse dipolar ESR spectroscopy can report on distances in the range from about 10 Å to as large as 80 Å or even longer in some cases.
source: In recent years, pulse dipolar ESR spectroscopy (PDS), in particular the double electron-electron resonance (DEER) method, utilizing spin labeling has become the method of choice for monitoring structural transitions in biological macromolecules and complexes by reporting on distances in the range from about 10 Å (Fafarman et al., 2007; Borbat et al., 2014) to as large as 80 Å (Borbat and Freed, 2007; Georgieva et al., 2008; Jeschke, 2012; Borbat et al., 2014) or even longer (Schmidt et al., 2016) in some cases.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.
